newsitem.title: USA: Gantt urges Helms to return foreign donations.
newsitem.headline: Gantt urges Helms to return foreign donations.

text.p: North Carolina Democrat Harvey Gantt, fighting to unseat Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, Wednesday denounced as "an outrage" donations by foreign governments to a foundation named in Helms' honour.

More than $300,000 was reported to have come from Taiwan and Kuwait to the foundation based at Helms' alma mater, Wingate University in Wingate, North Carolina. Helms, who has served in the U.S. Senate for 24 years, is chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
A statement from the Gantt campaign urged Helms to return the money and challenged him to release a list of contributors to the Jesse Helms Foundation, a tax-exempt organisation.

"These contributions that we have learned about are an outrage," Gantt said. "And I believe the people of North Carolina deserve to know what other foreign governments and big multinational corporations have given to Jesse Helms."

The Gantt campaign was responding to a recent Washington Post story that said the government of Taiwan donated $225,000 to the foundation after a conversation between Helms and a high-ranking Taiwanese official. It also said Kuwait donated $100,000 to the foundation after the Persian Gulf war.
"Who are the foreign governments, lobbyists and giant multinational corporations that he's been working for in Washington?" Gantt asked.
The Jesse Helms campaign dismissed the issue. "The Helms Centre is a private foundation, it has nothing to do with the campaign," spokeswoman Julie Wilkie said.

The Gantt-Helms contest is a rematch of their 1990 race that Helms won after a racially charged campaign. Gantt, 53, who became the first black mayor of Charlotte, is campaigning, in part, on promises of tax cuts for the middle class.
Political analysts said the issue of financial contributions was likely to have little impact on the race.

"Gantt is looking for any kind of leverage he can get against Helms. I don't think it will have much of an impact because the public is too cynical about campaign finance," said Paul Gronke, Duke University political science professor.
"Almost every campaign is going to have some donations that look shady. There's just too much money pouring in from a wide variety of sources," Gronke added.

Financial contributions from foreign sources have become an issue in the presidential race, with Republican Bob Dole and his aides blasting the fund-raising practices of the Democratic National Committee, particularly the activities of John Huang raising funds from Indonesian business interests.
